meta.title: Quiz 5 — Fetch API, REST & Async Patterns
meta.description: RESTful APIs, Fetch API, async/await, arrow functions, timers, and query parameters.

questions.questionMd: Based on the Spotify API example in the lecture, which URL would you use to retrieve data for an album with the Spotify ID `7aDBFWp72Pz4NZEtVBANi9`?

options.label: A
options.text: https://api.spotify.com/v1/search?type=album&id=7aDBFWp72Pz4NZEtVBANi9

options.label: B
options.text: https://api.spotify.com/v1/albums/7aDBFWp72Pz4NZEtVBANi9

options.label: C
options.text: https://developer.spotify.com/v1/albums?album_id=7aDBFWp72Pz4NZEtVBANi9

options.label: D
options.text: https://api.spotify.com/albums/7aDBFWp72Pz4NZEtVBANi9

questions.explanationMd: Spotify album resources are retrieved from the Web API base URL using the `/v1/albums/{id}` endpoint. The correct URL includes both `/v1` and `/albums/` followed by the album ID.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best describes a RESTful API?

options.label: A
options.text: A URL-based API where requests are sent as HTTP requests using methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to a base URL known as an API endpoint

options.label: B
options.text: A binary protocol API where data is encoded in a compact proprietary format and transmitted over persistent TCP connections without any HTTP overhead

options.label: C
options.text: A server-side scripting interface where the browser executes remote functions directly by sending the function name and arguments as query parameters

options.label: D
options.text: A peer-to-peer data exchange protocol where client and server negotiate a shared schema before any data transfer can begin

questions.explanationMd: A RESTful API exposes resources through URLs and uses HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to operate on those resources.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, why should you use `<input type="submit">` instead of `<button>` inside a form?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the 'submit' event fires when `<input type="submit">` is clicked but does not fire when a plain `<button>` element is clicked

options.label: B
options.text: Because `<input type="submit">` automatically calls `encodeURIComponent` on the input values before appending them to the request URL as query parameters

options.label: C
options.text: Because `<input type="submit">` is the only element that can be styled with CSS, whereas `<button>` elements inherit browser-specific default styles that cannot be overridden

options.label: D
options.text: Because `<button>` elements cause the browser to make a synchronous HTTP GET request on click, which blocks the JavaScript event loop until the server responds

questions.explanationMd: In the lecture's form-handling example, the submit control is used so the form's `submit` event is triggered and can be handled consistently by JavaScript.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what is the problem with using ordinary inner functions (closures) as callbacks in `fetch().then()` chains inside a class method?

options.label: A
options.text: The `fetch()` API enforces strict mode internally, which prevents closures from accessing any variable declared in the outer function scope with the `var` keyword

options.label: B
options.text: Closures capture the value of `this` at the time the outer function is defined rather than at the time it is called, leading to a stale reference in long-lived operations

options.label: C
options.text: Closures defined inside a method are garbage-collected before the `fetch()` promise resolves, causing a null reference error when the callback eventually fires

options.label: D
options.text: Each function has its own `this` value, so closures do not automatically inherit the `this` binding of their enclosing class method

questions.explanationMd: Ordinary functions create their own `this` binding based on how they are called. Inside a Promise callback, that can break access to the class instance unless the callback is bound or written as an arrow function.

questions.questionMd: Is it possible for a `fetch()` callback, such as `onJsonReady`, to fire in the middle of another function that is currently executing on the call stack?

options.label: A
options.text: It depends on the browser; some modern browsers implement speculative callback execution that can inject a microtask between two consecutive synchronous statements

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because Promises use the Micro-task Queue which has higher priority and is allowed to interrupt currently running synchronous code at any safe yield point

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only if the callback was registered with a timeout of zero milliseconds, which instructs the browser to fire it at the very next available CPU cycle

options.label: D
options.text: No, because JavaScript is single-threaded; a callback can only be placed on the call stack when the stack is empty

questions.explanationMd: JavaScript does not interrupt currently executing synchronous code. Asynchronous callbacks wait in a queue and are moved to the call stack only after the stack becomes empty.

questions.questionMd: In the JavaScript event loop model presented in the lecture, what is the role of the browser's internal implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the JavaScript engine's JIT compiler that translates JavaScript source code into machine code instructions that the CPU can execute directly without any further interpretation

options.label: B
options.text: It is the C++ code that executes in response to native JavaScript commands such as `setTimeout` and DOM manipulation methods

options.label: C
options.text: It is a sandboxed WebAssembly runtime that handles all memory-intensive operations to prevent the JavaScript heap from growing beyond the browser's allocated memory limit

options.label: D
options.text: It is the service worker layer that intercepts all network requests and decides whether to serve them from the cache or forward them to the actual remote server

questions.explanationMd: The browser provides native internal implementations for features such as timers and DOM operations. JavaScript calls into those browser-provided systems, which later schedule callbacks back into the event loop.

questions.questionMd: When handling a form's `submit` event in JavaScript, what must you call to prevent the page from refreshing?

options.label: A
options.text: window.cancelSubmit()

options.label: B
options.text: form.reset()

options.label: C
options.text: event.preventDefault()

options.label: D
options.text: event.stopPropagation()

questions.explanationMd: `event.preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default form submission behavior, preventing the page from reloading or navigating away.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, when does the browser's internal implementation add a task to the Task Queue?

options.label: A
options.text: When it determines that a callback from something like `setTimeout` or `addEventListener` should be fired, it creates a Task and enqueues it in the Task Queue

options.label: B
options.text: Whenever a variable assignment occurs inside an asynchronous callback, the assignment is deferred as a Task so that synchronous code always reads the previous value first

options.label: C
options.text: After each rendered frame, all pending DOM mutations are bundled into a single Task that the event loop must process before the browser can paint the next frame

options.label: D
options.text: Every time a new JavaScript function is declared anywhere in the code, whether as a named declaration or a function expression, a corresponding task entry is created immediately

questions.explanationMd: Browser APIs such as timers and event listeners schedule callbacks by adding tasks to the Task Queue when the relevant event or timer is ready.

questions.questionMd: When constructing a URL with query parameters, which character is used to separate the first query parameter from the base URL path?
questions.explanationMd: The first query parameter starts after a question mark (`?`). Additional query parameters are then separated with ampersands (`&`).

questions.questionMd: Consider this code: `console.log('A'); setTimeout(fn, 3000); console.log('B');` In what order will the console outputs appear?

options.label: A
options.text: The output from `fn`, then A, then B, because `setTimeout` callbacks are placed in the Micro-task Queue which has higher priority than synchronous code on the call stack

options.label: B
options.text: B, then A, then the output from `fn`, because the JavaScript engine hoists `setTimeout` calls to the top of the execution context before running any other statements

options.label: C
options.text: A, then the output from `fn` after 3 seconds, then B, because `setTimeout` blocks the call stack for the specified duration before allowing subsequent synchronous code to run

options.label: D
options.text: A, then B, then whatever `fn` logs after approximately 3 seconds

questions.explanationMd: `console.log('A')` and `console.log('B')` run synchronously first. `setTimeout` schedules `fn` to run later, after the delay and after the call stack is clear.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's Spotify example, what is the base URL for the Spotify Web API?

options.label: A
options.text: https://developer.spotify.com

options.label: B
options.text: https://data.spotify.com

options.label: C
options.text: https://api.spotify.com

options.label: D
options.text: https://music.spotify.com

questions.explanationMd: The Spotify Web API uses `https://api.spotify.com` as its base host. Versioned endpoints such as `/v1/albums/{id}` are appended to it.

questions.questionMd: In the context of JSON, what does it mean to deserialize a string?

options.label: A
options.text: To validate a JSON string against a predefined schema to ensure that all required fields are present and that their data types conform to the expected format

options.label: B
options.text: To turn a serialized string back into a usable JavaScript object

options.label: C
options.text: To strip whitespace and comments from a JSON string to reduce its size before transmitting it over a network connection with limited bandwidth

options.label: D
options.text: To encode a JavaScript object into a compact binary representation that can be stored efficiently in a key-value cache like Redis or Memcached

questions.explanationMd: Deserialization converts data from a string representation, such as JSON text, back into an object that code can use.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, RESTful API requests are sent with a specified MIME/content type. Which of the following is listed as a valid content type example?

options.label: A
options.text: YAML

options.label: B
options.text: GraphQL

options.label: C
options.text: JSON

options.label: D

questions.explanationMd: REST APIs commonly exchange data as JSON, typically represented by the MIME type `application/json`.

questions.questionMd: When using ordinary non-arrow inner functions as `fetch()` callbacks inside a class method, how can you correctly fix the `this` binding problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Assign the inner functions to class prototype properties before calling `fetch()`, so the JavaScript engine can look up the correct `this` through the prototype chain at call time

options.label: B
options.text: Declare the inner functions using the `var` keyword instead of `const` or `let`, because var-scoped functions automatically inherit the `this` context of their parent scope

options.label: C
options.text: Prefix the inner function declarations with the `static` keyword so that `this` inside the function always refers to the class constructor rather than an instance

options.label: D
options.text: Call `.bind(this)` on each inner function when passing it to `.then()`, so the enclosing method's `this` is explicitly attached to the callback

questions.explanationMd: `bind(this)` creates a new function whose `this` value is fixed to the current class instance, so the callback can safely access instance properties and methods.

questions.questionMd: By default, which type of request is blocked by the browser's CORS policy?

options.label: A
options.text: Same-origin requests made via `fetch()`, because the browser requires an explicit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: self` header even for same-domain calls

options.label: B
options.text: Cross-origin JavaScript files loaded with `<script src="...">`, which require the server to echo back the requesting origin in a special response header

options.label: C
options.text: Cross-origin CSS stylesheets loaded with `<link rel="stylesheet">`, which always trigger a preflight request before the stylesheet is applied to the DOM

options.label: D
options.text: Cross-origin requests made via `fetch()` or XHR

questions.explanationMd: Browsers restrict cross-origin `fetch()` and XMLHttpRequest calls unless the server explicitly allows the requesting origin through CORS response headers.

questions.questionMd: Why do all third-party REST APIs configure their servers to allow cross-origin `fetch()` requests?

options.label: A
options.text: Because CORS configuration is mandated by the HTTP/2 specification for any server that handles more than a certain number of simultaneous connections per second

options.label: B
options.text: Because configuring CORS on the server encrypts all cross-origin traffic using TLS, which protects API keys transmitted in request headers from being intercepted

options.label: C
options.text: Because browser vendors require all commercial APIs to register their domains in a public CORS whitelist maintained by the W3C before allowing cross-origin access

options.label: D
options.text: Because without that server-side configuration, browsers would block cross-origin `fetch()` calls and external developers would not be able to access the API at all

questions.explanationMd: CORS is enforced by browsers. Third-party APIs must send the right CORS headers so browser-based applications from other origins can call them.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, when comparing the priority of the Micro-task Queue and the Task Queue, which one does the Event Loop process first?

options.label: A
options.text: The Task Queue has higher priority because it handles user-visible interactions such as click and input events that must be processed before invisible background Promise callbacks

options.label: B
options.text: Priority is determined dynamically based on the age of each queued task, so the oldest task regardless of which queue it belongs to is always processed next

options.label: C
options.text: Both queues have equal priority and the Event Loop alternates between them in a strict round-robin fashion, taking one task from each queue per iteration of the loop

options.label: D
options.text: The Micro-task Queue has higher priority than the Task Queue and is processed first

questions.explanationMd: Promise callbacks are placed in the microtask queue, which is drained before the event loop moves on to the next regular task.

questions.questionMd: What is the key advantage of using arrow functions (`=>`) as callbacks in `fetch().then()` chains compared to ordinary functions?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrow functions bypass the browser's CORS policy because they use a different internal request mechanism that does not carry an Origin header in the HTTP request

options.label: B
options.text: Arrow functions are automatically bound to the `this` value of their enclosing context, so they do not create their own `this` binding

options.label: C
options.text: Arrow functions execute synchronously instead of asynchronously, which ensures that the callback completes before any subsequent line of code in the method runs

options.label: D
options.text: Arrow functions convert the Promise returned by `fetch()` into a plain value synchronously, eliminating the need for chained `.then()` calls in most use cases

questions.explanationMd: Arrow functions use lexical `this`, meaning they keep the `this` value from the surrounding scope instead of creating their own callback-specific binding.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what type of HTTP request does a browser issue when you load a URL by typing it into the address bar?

options.label: A
options.text: An HTTP POST request, because navigation events send the current page's form state to the server as part of the browser's session continuity mechanism

options.label: B
options.text: An HTTP OPTIONS request, so that the browser can first discover which methods and content types the destination server supports before committing to a full request

options.label: C
options.text: An HTTP GET request for the resource at that URL

options.label: D
options.text: An HTTP HEAD request that retrieves only the response headers so the browser can determine the content type and size before deciding to download the full body

questions.explanationMd: Typing a URL into the address bar requests the resource with the HTTP GET method, which asks the server to return the representation at that URL.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what is the general problem referred to loosely as a 'race condition' in single-threaded JavaScript?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple JavaScript threads execute the same callback simultaneously, each modifying shared memory in a way that produces an inconsistent final state

options.label: B
options.text: Two `fetch()` calls are dispatched simultaneously and whichever response arrives first overwrites the state set by the slower response, producing corrupted UI data

options.label: C
options.text: There are two or more events that can occur at unpredictable times and those events are dependent on each other in some way

options.label: D
options.text: The browser's rendering engine and the JavaScript engine compete for CPU time, causing visible frame drops whenever a complex DOM update is triggered by a fetch callback

questions.explanationMd: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing or ordering of events that are not fully predictable. Even single-threaded JavaScript can have this issue with asynchronous events.

questions.questionMd: In a URL query string, how are query parameter key-value pairs structured?

options.label: A
options.text: Each pair is formatted as `param/value` using a slash separator, following the hierarchical path convention used in the base URL segment of RESTful API endpoints

options.label: B
options.text: Each pair is formatted as `{param, value}` using curly-brace destructuring syntax borrowed from JavaScript ES6 to maintain consistency with the client-side code that builds the URL

options.label: C
options.text: Each pair is formatted as `param:value` using a colon separator, consistent with the JSON object notation used in the response body returned by RESTful endpoints

options.label: D
options.text: Each pair is formatted as `param=value`, where the parameter name and its value are separated by an equals sign

questions.explanationMd: Query strings represent each key-value pair as `name=value`. Multiple pairs are usually joined with `&`.

questions.questionMd: In the context of JSON, what does it mean to serialize an object?

options.label: A
options.text: To send an object directly over a network socket without any intermediate text representation or encoding step

options.label: B
options.text: To turn an object into a string that can later be deserialized

options.label: C
options.text: To compress a JavaScript object into a binary format suitable for storage in a relational database column

options.label: D
options.text: To convert a plain-text string into a fully constructed JavaScript object complete with methods and prototype chain

questions.explanationMd: Serialization converts an object into a storable or transferable representation such as a JSON string. That string can later be deserialized back into data.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's definition, what is a 'gotcha' in programming?

options.label: A
options.text: A security vulnerability in a programming language runtime that attackers can exploit to execute arbitrary code by supplying malformed input to a parsing function

options.label: B
options.text: A deliberate bug intentionally left in a codebase by a developer to test whether automated testing pipelines are comprehensive enough to catch subtle logic errors

options.label: C
options.text: A valid construct that works as documented but is counter-intuitive and almost invites mistakes because it is easy to invoke and unexpected in its outcome

options.label: D
options.text: A deprecated API function that still exists in the language specification for backward compatibility but produces incorrect results when called in strict mode environments

questions.explanationMd: A programming gotcha is a valid language feature or behavior that is easy to use incorrectly because it produces surprising or counter-intuitive results.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which type of resource can be loaded cross-origin by default without triggering a CORS error?

options.label: A
options.text: JSON data fetched using the `fetch()` API from a different domain, provided the `Content-Type` response header is set to `application/json`

options.label: B
options.text: Images loaded via an `` tag

options.label: C
options.text: XHR (`XMLHttpRequest`) responses from external servers, which were exempted from CORS restrictions in the original XMLHttpRequest Level 1 specification

options.label: D
options.text: WebSocket connections to external domains, because WebSocket uses a different handshake protocol that bypasses the standard browser same-origin policy

questions.explanationMd: Browsers generally allow resources such as images to be embedded from other origins with an `` tag. Programmatic access to cross-origin data through `fetch()` or XHR is more restricted.

questions.questionMd: What does it mean that JavaScript is 'single-threaded'?

options.label: A
options.text: JavaScript processes only one file at a time, so all external script tags are loaded and executed in strict source-order before any user events are processed

options.label: B
options.text: JavaScript can execute multiple functions simultaneously as long as they are declared as async, because the async keyword spawns a separate execution thread for each call

options.label: C
options.text: JavaScript shares a single CPU core with the browser's rendering engine but uses time-slicing to interleave rendering and script execution within each frame budget

options.label: D
options.text: There is one call stack, so JavaScript can only process one command at a time

questions.explanationMd: Single-threaded JavaScript means the main JavaScript execution context uses one call stack and runs one piece of code at a time.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, why can multiple images load in parallel even though JavaScript is single-threaded?

options.label: A
options.text: The browser batches all image requests into a single multiplexed HTTP/2 stream that the JavaScript engine processes sequentially but displays simultaneously after all bytes arrive

options.label: B
options.text: JavaScript uses Web Workers internally for all image element operations, with each Image object spawning its own dedicated worker thread to manage the download lifecycle

options.label: C
options.text: The browser itself is multi-threaded and multi-process, so network requests and image decoding happen in browser threads outside the JavaScript runtime

options.label: D
options.text: Image loading is handled entirely by the operating system's DNS resolver and network stack, which feeds completed image buffers directly into the browser's graphics memory

questions.explanationMd: JavaScript on the main thread runs one command at a time, but the browser has other threads and processes for networking, decoding, and rendering resources in parallel.

questions.questionMd: In JavaScript, how do you read the current text entered by a user in an `<input type="text">` element?

options.label: A
options.text: inputElement.innerHTML

options.label: B
options.text: inputElement.textContent

options.label: C
options.text: inputElement.data

options.label: D
options.text: inputElement.value

questions.explanationMd: For form input elements, the current user-entered value is stored in the element's `value` property.

questions.questionMd: When using the Fetch API, which method should you call on a response object to automatically parse the response body as JSON?

options.label: A
options.text: response.parse(), a built-in Fetch helper that detects the Content-Type header and chooses the appropriate parsing strategy automatically

options.label: B
options.text: response.decode(), which handles base64-encoded JSON payloads by first decoding them and then running a standard JSON parser on the result

options.label: C
options.text: response.json()

options.label: D
options.text: response.text(), which returns the raw string and requires you to manually call `JSON.parse()` in a separate subsequent step

questions.explanationMd: The Fetch API's `Response` object provides `response.json()`, which reads the response body and parses it as JSON, returning a Promise for the parsed value.

questions.questionMd: What does the acronym JSON stand for?

options.label: A
options.text: JavaScript Oriented Networking

options.label: B
options.text: Joint Serialization Of Nodes

options.label: C
options.text: Java Standardized Object Notation

options.label: D
options.text: JavaScript Object Notation

questions.explanationMd: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation, a text-based data format commonly used for exchanging structured data.

questions.questionMd: If a page at `abc.com/users` makes a `fetch()` request to `abc.com/search`, how is this request classified according to CORS rules?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a same-origin request because both URLs share the same domain

options.label: B
options.text: It is a cross-origin request because the URL paths `/users` and `/search` are different, which triggers the browser's preflight OPTIONS mechanism

options.label: C
options.text: It is a cross-origin request because `fetch()` always performs an origin check against the `window.location.href` value at the time the call is initiated

options.label: D
options.text: It is classified as a restricted request because it travels between two different endpoints on the server, which requires an explicit `Access-Control-Allow-Path` header

questions.explanationMd: CORS is based on origin, which is determined by scheme, host, and port. Different paths on the same domain are still considered same-origin, assuming the scheme and port are also the same.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what characterizes a multi-threaded execution environment?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple commands are processed simultaneously and there is one call stack per thread

options.label: B
options.text: Commands are processed one at a time but each command runs inside its own isolated memory sandbox so that variable mutations in one command cannot affect another

options.label: C
options.text: A single call stack is shared among all active execution contexts, with a scheduler deciding which context gets CPU time on each clock cycle

options.label: D
options.text: The event loop distributes microtasks and macrotasks across a pool of worker processes, each of which maintains a separate heap but shares the same call stack

questions.explanationMd: In a multi-threaded environment, multiple threads can execute commands at the same time, and each thread has its own call stack.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, in which year did Facebook open-source GraphQL?
questions.explanationMd: According to the lecture material, Facebook open-sourced GraphQL in 2015.

questions.questionMd: To allow a form to submit when the user presses the Enter key, in addition to clicking a button, what must you do in your HTML?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a `keydown` event listener directly to the input element and manually check whether the key pressed has the code value of `Enter` each time a keystroke occurs

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap the input elements inside a `<form>` element and listen for the `submit` event on that form

options.label: C
options.text: Set the `autocomplete` attribute on the input element to `on` so that the browser automatically triggers submission when it detects a confirmed input value

options.label: D
options.text: Use a `<button type="button">` element paired with a global document-level `keypress` listener that checks for the Enter key on every page interaction

questions.explanationMd: Putting the inputs inside a `<form>` lets the browser trigger the form's `submit` event when the user presses Enter, so the same submit handler can handle both Enter and button submission.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what is a simple way to check whether a particular company or product offers a publicly accessible developer API?

options.label: A
options.text: Search for `<product name> API` using a search engine to see if a developer API exists

options.label: B
options.text: Send an HTTP OPTIONS request to the company's main domain and inspect the Allow header in the response to discover the supported API endpoints and methods

options.label: C
options.text: Check the W3C's official registry of public REST APIs, which every company is required to register with before making its API available to third-party developers

options.label: D
options.text: Use the browser's Network tab to inspect all requests made by the company's website, then reverse-engineer those endpoints to determine which ones accept external calls

questions.explanationMd: A practical first step is to search for the product or company name together with `API`, which often leads to official developer documentation if one exists.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which company introduced Falcor as a REST alternative?

options.label: A
options.text: Amazon, which required a uniform data-access abstraction across its many distributed AWS services that had diverse underlying data formats

options.label: B
options.text: Netflix

options.label: C
options.text: Facebook, which needed a declarative data-fetching layer for its React-based front-end after experiencing performance problems with traditional REST endpoints

options.label: D
options.text: Microsoft, which built it as an open-source project to simplify data binding between Azure cloud services and JavaScript single-page applications

questions.explanationMd: Falcor is associated with Netflix and was introduced as an alternative model for accessing remote data.

questions.questionMd: What HTTP method does the `fetch()` API use by default when no options object is provided?

options.label: A
options.text: HEAD

options.label: B
options.text: POST

options.label: C
options.text: GET

options.label: D
options.text: OPTIONS

questions.explanationMd: A basic `fetch(url)` request uses the HTTP `GET` method unless another method is specified in the options object.

questions.questionMd: In a URL query string, which character separates subsequent non-first query parameters from each other?

options.label: A
options.text: `;` (semicolon)

options.label: B
options.text: `=` (equals sign)

questions.explanationMd: After the first query parameter begins with `?`, additional query parameters are separated with `&`, for example `?q=test&page=2`.
